why: In A a single square holds a double circle. In B the two shapes come apart and overlap, and the double outline jumps to the other shape: the circle becomes single at top-left and the square becomes double at bottom-right. In C a single circle holds a double triangle, so we need a single triangle at top-left and a double circle at bottom-right, which is option 4. Option 3 is tempting but its triangle is still double.
trick: Count single and double outlines for every shape; this is often the whole rule.
note: In A the outer shape is a single square and the inner a double circle, but B shows a single circle and a double square, so the double outline moves from one shape to the other. Same rule applied to C gives option 4, matching the book.
